q: Wednesday evening club race, a mixed fleet of ILCA 7s. You are reaching behind the line when the committee boat hoists the class flag with one sound. The notice of race says nothing unusual about the starting sequence. What has just happened and when is your start?
a: That was the warning signal — the starting signal comes 5 minutes later
o: That was the preparatory signal — the starting signal comes 4 minutes later
That was the one-minute signal — start your watch for 60 seconds
That was the starting signal — the class flag goes up when the race starts
why: Rule 26: the class flag with one sound is the warning signal, 5 minutes before the start unless the NoR or SI say otherwise.

q: A 470 national championship, 25 knots and waves. Four minutes before the start the committee boat hoists flag P with one sound. Your crew says the rules of Part 2 don't bite yet because the race hasn't started. From which moment are you actually racing, with everything that implies for penalties?
a: From this preparatory signal — a boat is racing from her preparatory signal until she finishes and clears the line
o: From the warning signal five minutes before the start, when the class flag went up
From the starting signal — before it you are not racing and cannot be penalised
From the moment you cross the starting line after the starting signal
why: Definition Racing: a boat is racing from her preparatory signal; rule 26: the preparatory flag is P, I, Z, U or black.

fig.title: Four minutes to go
lines: Flag P hoisted with one sound

q: Lake regatta, J/24s, a light 6-knot breeze. You see flag P come down on the committee boat and hear one long sound. The class flag is still flying. How long until your starting signal?
a: One minute — lowering the preparatory flag with one long sound is the one-minute signal
o: Four minutes — the preparatory flag comes down four minutes before the start
Zero — the long sound is the starting signal; cross the line now
Five minutes — the long sound restarts the sequence from the warning
why: Rule 26: the preparatory flag is removed one minute before the start with one long sound.

q: Saronic Gulf, a cruiser-racer regatta. You are hovering a boat length below the line. The class flag is lowered on the committee boat and you hear one sound. Flag P came down a minute ago. What does this signal mean?
a: It is the starting signal — the class flag removed with one sound
o: It is the one-minute signal — the sequence ends in 60 seconds
It is a postponement — the class flag down means wait for a new sequence
It is a general recall — everybody returns behind the line
why: Rule 26: at 0 minutes the class flag is removed with one sound — that is the starting signal.

q: Your crew on a Melges 24 missed the sequence while sorting a halyard. You look up: the preparatory flag came down 20 seconds ago, the class flag is still flying, no other flags. How long do you have until the starting signal?
a: 40 seconds — the preparatory flag comes down at one minute, so the start is 40 seconds away
o: 3 minutes 40 seconds — the preparatory flag comes down at four minutes
4 minutes 40 seconds — the preparatory flag comes down at five minutes
You cannot tell — only the sound signals give the time
why: Rule 26: the preparatory flag is removed at 1 minute; 60 s minus 20 s leaves 40 s to the start.

q: A trapezoid course off Bodrum. Your timer shows that the class flag went up exactly 2 minutes 30 seconds ago. Flag P is still flying. With the standard sequence, how long to the start and when will P come down?
a: 2 minutes 30 seconds to the start; flag P comes down in 1 minute 30 seconds
o: 1 minute 30 seconds to the start; flag P comes down in 30 seconds
3 minutes 30 seconds to the start; flag P comes down in 2 minutes 30 seconds
2 minutes 30 seconds to the start; flag P comes down at the starting signal
why: Rule 26: warning at 5 min, preparatory flag down at 1 min — 5:00 minus 2:30 is 2:30, and P drops 1:30 from now.

fig.title: Your timer
lines: Class flag up 2 min 30 s ago

q: A windy start on a river. You see flag P come down on the committee boat but hear no horn — the air horn has failed. Your helm says the sequence is void without the sound. What is the correct position?
a: The start is one minute away — times are taken from the visual signals and the absence of a sound is disregarded
o: The sequence is void — the race committee must postpone and restart the sequence
Nothing has happened — a signal without its sound has no effect
The one-minute signal counts only if the race committee hails the time instead
why: Rule 26: times shall be taken from the visual signals; the absence of a sound signal shall be disregarded.

q: Palma, a 36-ft cruiser-racer. Your stopwatch, started at the warning, reads 5:00 and you hear a horn from a neighbouring boat, but the class flag is still flying on the committee boat. Your tactician shouts "Go!". Have you been given the starting signal?
a: No — the starting signal is the removal of the class flag; a horn without it is not the start
o: Yes — five minutes after the warning the race has started whatever the flag shows
Yes — any sound signal at the expected time is the starting signal
No — the start is only when the committee boat hails "Start" on the radio
why: Rule 26: times are taken from the visual signals; the starting signal is the class flag being removed.

q: Two fleets at a lake championship: ILCA 7 then 470. At 12:00:00 the ILCA class flag comes down with one sound and, at the same moment, the 470 class flag goes up with another sound. A 470 sailor complains that two signals cannot be made at once. Is the committee right?
a: Yes — the warning signal of a following class is made with or after the starting signal of the preceding class
o: No — the warning signal of the next class must wait at least one minute after the previous start
No — the next class's warning signal can only be made after its preparatory signal
Yes, but only if both classes share the same preparatory flag
why: Rule 26: the warning signal for each succeeding class shall be made with or after the starting signal of the preceding class.

lines: ILCA class flag lowered, one sound

q: Four minutes before the start of a 29er fleet the committee boat hoists flag I instead of flag P. Your crew asks what changes for you compared with a normal P-flag start.
a: If any part of your hull is on the course side in the last minute, you must sail round an end of the line to the pre-start side before starting
o: Nothing — flag I is just another preparatory flag; you may dip back across the line if you are over
If you are over in the last minute you get a 20 % scoring penalty without a hearing
If you are over in the last minute you are disqualified without a hearing
why: Rule 30.1: under flag I a boat on the course side in the last minute must sail across an extension of the line to the pre-start side before she starts.

q: Big fleet of Optimists at a national event. At the preparatory signal the committee boat displays flag Z. Your coach asked you yesterday to know every preparatory flag. Which rule is now in force?
a: Rule 30.2 — a 20 % scoring penalty for a boat in the triangle in the last minute
o: Rule 30.1 — a boat over in the last minute must return round an end
Rule 30.3 — disqualification unless the race is restarted or resailed
Rule 30.4 — disqualification that survives a general recall
why: Race signals: flag Z means rule 30.2 is in effect.

q: After two general recalls of a 90-boat ILCA 6 fleet the committee boat shows a black rectangular flag as the preparatory signal. What does it mean for the last minute before the start?
a: Rule 30.4 applies — a boat identified in the triangle in the last minute is disqualified without a hearing, even if the race is recalled again
o: Rule 30.3 applies — disqualification only if this attempt is not recalled
Rule 30.1 applies — a boat over in the last minute must round an end to return
Rule 30.2 applies — a boat over in the last minute gets a 20 % scoring penalty
why: Race signals: the black flag means rule 30.4 is in effect — the penalty survives a general recall.

q: Split regatta, 20 knots. At four minutes the committee boat hoists flag U with one sound. A crew member who sails only club races asks what the U flag does.
a: Rule 30.3 — a boat in the triangle in the last minute is disqualified without a hearing unless the race is restarted or resailed
o: Rule 30.4 — disqualification that stands even after a general recall
Rule 30.2 — a 20 % scoring penalty without a hearing
Rule 30.1 — a boat over in the last minute must return round an end of the line
why: Race signals: flag U means rule 30.3 is in effect.

q: The notice of race for a J/70 event says: "Races will be started using rule 26 with the warning signal made 3 minutes before the starting signal." At 13:57:00 your class flag goes up with one sound. When is your start?
a: 14:00:00 — the notice of race may change the 5-minute interval, and the rest of the sequence is as in rule 26
o: 14:02:00 — the warning is always 5 minutes before the start
13:58:00 — with a 3-minute warning the preparatory signal is the start
The sequence is invalid — rule 26 cannot be changed by the notice of race
why: Rule 26: the warning signal is 5 minutes before the start "or as stated in the notice of race or sailing instructions".

q: Two minutes before your warning signal the wind drops to 3 knots. The committee boat hoists flag AP with two sounds. Your helm wants to head for the harbour for coffee. What does the signal tell you?
a: Races not started are postponed; the warning signal will be made one minute after AP is lowered — stay near the line
o: Racing is over for today — you may go ashore
Races are abandoned; the sequence will restart one hour later
The race is postponed and further signals will be made ashore
why: Race signals, AP: races not started are postponed; the warning signal will be made 1 minute after removal unless postponed again or abandoned.

fig.title: Two minutes before the warning
lines: No pennant or other flag under it

q: A Dragon regatta on a windless morning. Flag AP has been flying for an hour. At 11:40:00 it is lowered with one sound. Assuming the standard sequence, when is the warning signal and when is the start?
a: Warning at 11:41:00, start at 11:46:00
o: Warning at 11:40:00, start at 11:45:00
Warning at 11:45:00, start at 11:50:00
Warning at 11:41:00, start at 11:45:00
why: Race signals, AP: the warning signal is made 1 minute after AP is lowered; rule 26: the start is 5 minutes after the warning.

q: The first start of the day is scheduled for 11:00. At 10:30 the committee boat ashore shows AP over numeral pennant 2 with two sounds. What does the race committee mean?
a: Races are postponed 2 hours — the scheduled start is now 13:00
o: Race 2 is postponed; race 1 will be started on time
Races are postponed for 2 minutes after the flag is lowered
Two more general recalls will be followed by a black-flag start
why: Race signals: AP over a numeral pennant 1–9 postpones races by that many hours from the scheduled starting time.
ref: RRS race signals (AP over numeral pennant)

q: After waiting all afternoon for wind, you see the committee boat hoist flag AP over flag A with two sounds. What should the fleet do?
a: Go ashore — races not started are postponed and there will be no more racing today
o: Stay near the line — the warning signal comes one minute after the flags are lowered
Return to the starting area — all races in progress are abandoned and will be resailed
Listen on the VHF — further signals will be made by radio in one hour
why: Race signals: AP over A means races not started are postponed and no more racing today.

q: Thunderstorms are forecast. Before the first warning signal the committee boat displays AP over H with two sounds and starts her engine. What are you being told?
a: Races not started are postponed and further signals will be made ashore — go in and watch the official notice board
o: Races are postponed; the warning signal will come one minute after the flags are lowered
Races are postponed and there will be no more racing today
All boats must return to the harbour and the race is abandoned
why: Race signals: AP over H means races not started are postponed; further signals ashore.

q: Ten minutes into the first beat of a club race the wind swings 60° and dies. A mark boat passes the fleet with flag N and you hear three sounds. What does the signal mean for you?
a: All races in progress are abandoned — return to the starting area; a warning signal will follow one minute after N is lowered
o: The course is shortened — finish at the next mark and the race will be scored
Your race continues; only the classes that have not yet started are postponed
Racing is over for today — all races are abandoned and you may go ashore
why: Race signals, N: all races that have started are abandoned, return to the starting area; the warning signal follows 1 minute after N is lowered.

fig.title: On the first beat
lines: Flag N on a committee vessel

q: A squall line arrives during the second race and the committee boat shows N over A with three sounds. What now?
a: All races in progress are abandoned and there is no more racing today — head for the harbour
o: The race is abandoned; a new warning signal will be made one minute after the flags come down
The race is abandoned; further signals will be made ashore
Only the race in progress is abandoned; the next race starts as scheduled
why: Race signals: N over A means all races abandoned, no more racing today.

q: During a Hobie 16 race a thick fog bank rolls in. The committee boat shows N over H with three sounds. What has the race committee decided?
a: All races in progress are abandoned; further signals will be made ashore
o: All races are abandoned and there will be no more racing today
The race is abandoned; the warning signal will be made one minute after the flags are lowered
The race continues but the next leg is changed; watch for the new bearing
why: Race signals: N over H means all races abandoned, further signals ashore.

q: You are sailing to the starting area for a Star-class race when the committee boat hoists flag L and sounds a horn. Nothing is posted on the notice board you can see. What should you do?
a: Come within hail of the committee boat or follow her — afloat, flag L means that
o: Wear your personal flotation device — flag L means the safety rule is in force
Return to the harbour — flag L means racing is cancelled for the day
Start your watch — flag L is the warning signal for the first class
why: Race signals: flag L afloat means "come within hail or follow this vessel"; ashore it means a notice to competitors has been posted.

q: At the warning signal of a 470 race in 25 knots, the committee boat also hoists flag Y with one sound. One of your crew has unclipped his buoyancy aid to adjust his trapeze harness. What does flag Y require?
a: Everyone must wear a personal flotation device at all times during this race, except briefly while changing or adjusting clothing or personal equipment
o: Only the helm must wear a personal flotation device; the crew may choose
Personal flotation devices are recommended but not compulsory until the start
Flag Y is the preparatory signal — nothing to do with buoyancy aids
why: Rule 40.2(a): flag Y with one sound before or with the warning signal makes rule 40.1 apply for that race; rule 27.1 lets the RC signal it.

q: The sailing instructions say: "The starting line is between a staff displaying an orange flag on the committee boat and the course side of the port-end mark." You are lining up on starboard near the committee boat. Where exactly is the line at the committee-boat end?
a: At the staff with the orange flag — not at the committee boat's bow or stern
o: At the bow of the committee boat, the nearest point to the course
At the stern of the committee boat, where the race officer stands
Anywhere alongside the committee boat — she is a mark, so any part of her counts
why: Race signals: the orange flag on a staff marks one end of the starting line; the SI define the line from that staff.

fig.note: Line from the pin to the orange-flag staff on the RC boat

q: Thirty seconds before the warning signal of a windward–leeward race the committee boat swaps the course board from "W2" to "W3" and sounds a horn. A competitor near you protests loudly that the course cannot be changed once boats are on the water. Who is right?
a: The race committee — it may replace one course signal with another no later than the warning signal
o: The competitor — the course may only be changed by the sailing instructions, never by a signal
The competitor — the course is fixed once the first boat has left the harbour
The race committee, but only if it also postpones and starts a new sequence
why: Rule 27.1: no later than the warning signal the RC shall signal the course if not in the SI, and may replace one course signal with another.

q: Three minutes before the start of a J/24 race — after the preparatory signal — the pin-end mark boat picks up the pin and re-lays it 40 m further to windward because the line was badly skewed. You had set up for the old pin. Was the race committee entitled to do this?
a: No — a starting mark may be moved no later than the preparatory signal; if the move made your score significantly worse you may request redress
o: Yes — the race committee may move a starting mark at any time before the starting signal
Yes — the race committee may move a starting mark until one minute before the start
No — a starting mark may never be moved after the warning signal
why: Rule 27.2: the RC may move a starting mark no later than the preparatory signal; an improper action is a ground for redress under 61.4(b)(1).

q: Thirty seconds before the start of a Dragon race the wind shifts 40° to the right, turning the first leg into a fetch. The committee boat hoists AP with two sounds. Your tactician says the race committee cannot postpone once the preparatory signal has been made. Is she right?
a: No — before the starting signal the race committee may postpone for any reason, including a shift that spoils the beat
o: Yes — after the preparatory signal the race may only be abandoned, not postponed
Yes — a postponement in the last minute is only allowed for a safety reason
No — but the race committee must first finish the sequence and then recall the fleet
why: Rule 27.3: before the starting signal the RC may for any reason postpone (AP, AP over H or AP over A with two sounds) or abandon the race.

q: Ten seconds before the start of an Optimist race the committee boat notices the windward mark has broken free and is drifting away. It displays flag N with three sounds. One coach shouts that the race should have been started and shortened later. Which action was correct?
a: Flag N — before the starting signal the race committee may abandon the race for any reason, with three sounds
o: AP — a race may only be postponed, not abandoned, before its start
Start the race and then abandon it — abandonment is only possible after the starting signal
Flag M on the committee boat — the committee boat becomes the windward mark
why: Rule 27.3: before the starting signal the RC may abandon the race for any reason by displaying N, N over H or N over A with three sounds.

q: P-flag start in a 20-boat Melges 24 fleet. At the gun your bow is half a metre over the line. You bear away, cross back behind the line until the whole hull is on the pre-start side, then harden up and cross again. Have you started?
a: Yes — you started the moment your hull crossed the line the second time, having been entirely on the pre-start side after the starting signal
o: No — once over the line at the gun you must sail round an end of the line before you can start
No — you started the first time you crossed, but you are OCS and cannot cure it
Yes — you started at the gun; the second crossing was unnecessary
why: Definition Start: a boat starts when her hull crosses the line from the pre-start side after being entirely on that side at or after the starting signal.

fig.note: Over at the gun, back below the line, up again

q: You sail a sportsboat with a 1.5-m fixed bowsprit. At the starting signal the bowsprit is clearly across the line but the stem of the hull is 30 cm behind it. The committee boat shows no flag X. A rival hails that you were over. Were you?
a: No — the definition of Start and rule 29.1 refer to the hull; a bowsprit or crew across the line does not make you OCS
o: Yes — any part of the boat or her equipment over the line at the signal makes her OCS
Yes — the bowsprit is part of the hull for the purpose of starting
No, but only because the committee boat did not display flag X
why: Definition Start / rule 29.1: it is the hull that must be behind the line at the starting signal — not equipment or crew.

fig.note: Bowsprit over, hull behind at the gun

q: Crowded committee-boat end, 30 knots, a 36-ft cruiser-racer. Squeezed out at the gun, you pass to windward of the committee boat — outside the line — and then bear away onto the first beat. Your hull was entirely behind the line's extension at the signal. Have you started?
a: No — to start you must cross the starting line itself between its ends; sail back to the pre-start side and cross the line properly
o: Yes — you were on the pre-start side at the signal and are now on the course side
Yes — passing outside the committee boat is a legal "round-the-end" start
No — and because you passed the committee boat you must take a one-turn penalty before returning
why: Definition Start, rule 28.1: a boat starts by crossing the starting line from the pre-start side; sailing round the committee boat does not start her.

fig.note: You passed outside the RC boat at the gun

q: P-flag start, a river with current pushing the fleet over. You are OCS at the gun near the middle of a 300-m line and flag X goes up. What is the quickest legal way to start?
a: Sail back across the line by any route until your hull is entirely on the pre-start side, keeping clear of boats that are starting correctly, then start
o: Sail round the pin or the committee boat to the pre-start side — dipping back across the line is not allowed
Take a two-turns penalty on the course side and carry on racing
Keep racing — flag X is only a warning and the committee may accept your start
why: Under flag P a recalled boat may return across the line (definition Start); rule 21.1: while returning she keeps clear of boats not doing so.

fig.note: Flag X is up; you were over at the gun

q: Club race, 40 Lasers. After the start flag X is displayed with one sound, but the race officer hails only "4471 and 1823". Your number is 2206 and you were over too. Your friend says you are fine because you were not called. Must you return?
a: Yes — flag X with one sound is the individual recall; the race committee is not required to hail sail numbers, and the duty to start correctly is yours
o: No — only boats whose sail numbers are hailed are recalled
No — if the race committee hails some numbers and not yours, it has accepted your start
Yes, but only if the hail was made within 30 seconds of the starting signal
why: Rule 29.1 requires only flag X with one sound; hailing numbers is not required, and a boat that does not start correctly is scored OCS.

q: You know you were over at the start of an ILCA 7 race and flag X is flying. You decide to "see what happens" and keep sailing. Four minutes after the starting signal flag X comes down. Your training partner says the committee has now accepted everyone who is still on the course. Is that right?
a: No — flag X must come down no later than 4 minutes after the start regardless of who has returned; you will be scored OCS
o: Yes — lowering flag X means all recalled boats have returned or been accepted
Yes — after 4 minutes an OCS boat can no longer be penalised
No — but you may still return and start until the first boat reaches the windward mark
why: Rule 29.1: flag X is displayed until all recalled boats have returned, but no later than 4 minutes after the start; a boat that did not start is scored OCS.

q: Two classes start five minutes apart. After the first start flag X is hoisted for several OCS boats. Three minutes after that start, with two boats still not back, the race committee lowers flag X. One of them later asks for redress, saying the flag was taken down too early. Was it?
a: No — flag X comes down no later than 4 minutes after the start or 1 minute before the next starting signal, whichever is earlier; here that is 3 minutes
o: Yes — flag X must stay up for a full 4 minutes after the starting signal
Yes — flag X must stay up until every recalled boat has returned
No — flag X may be lowered at any time once the first boat has been identified
why: Rule 29.1: flag X stays up until all have returned, but no later than 4 min after the start or 1 min before any later starting signal, whichever is earlier.

q: Pin-end start in a 60-boat Optimist fleet. You are sure your bow was a metre over at the signal, but no flag X is displayed and no sound is made — the committee did not see you. What should you do?
a: Go back and start correctly — until you do, you have not started; if you carry on, you have not sailed the course and should retire
o: Keep racing — without flag X you have started correctly by definition
Take a two-turns penalty when convenient; that cures a starting error
Keep racing and tell the race committee after finishing so it can add a 20 % penalty
why: Definition Start, rule 28.1: a boat over at the signal has not started until she returns and crosses again; the flag is the RC's duty, starting is hers.
ref: RRS definition Start, RRS 28.1, Basic Principle Sportsmanship

q: The results of race 3 show you OCS. You are certain you were behind the line — your crew filmed the start from the bow. You ask the race office for a protest hearing against the race committee. What is the right procedure?
a: Request redress within the time limit — the race committee scores OCS without a hearing, and a wrong scoring is an improper action to be corrected through redress
o: Protest the race committee under rule 60 — a protest form with a red flag is required
Nothing can be done — a scoring decision of the race committee is final
Ask the race committee to hold a hearing on the water with the two boats nearest you as witnesses
why: Rule A5: the RC scores OCS without a hearing; rule 61.4(b)(1): an improper action or omission of the RC is remedied through a request for redress.

fig.title: Results, race 3
lines: You believe you were behind the line

q: You were OCS and are sailing back to the pre-start side on port tack after the starting signal. Blue, who started correctly, is close-hauled on starboard and heading for you. Who must keep clear?
a: You — a boat sailing toward the pre-start side to start keeps clear of a boat that is not doing so, until her hull is entirely on the pre-start side
o: Blue — she must keep clear of a boat that is returning to start, as she would of a boat taking a penalty
Both equally — the port–starboard rule is suspended while boats are returning
Blue — a boat that has started is clear ahead in the race and must give room to boats behind her
why: Rule 21.1: a boat sailing toward the pre-start side after her starting signal keeps clear of a boat not doing so until her hull is entirely on that side.

fig.note: You are returning after the gun; Blue has started

q: You were OCS, returned and are now entirely on the pre-start side, sailing close-hauled on starboard tack towards the line to start. Red, who was late to the line, is approaching on port tack and hails "You were over — keep clear of me!" Who keeps clear now?
a: Red — rule 21.1 stopped applying to you when your hull was entirely on the pre-start side; you are now simply a starboard-tack boat under rule 10
o: You — a boat that was OCS keeps clear of all other boats until she has started
You — a boat that was OCS must keep clear until she has crossed the line and cleared it
Red, but only because she hailed; without the hail you would have to keep clear
why: Rule 21.1 applies only until the returning boat's hull is entirely on the pre-start side; after that the ordinary Part 2 rules apply — here rule 10.

fig.note: You are fully back below the line

q: A 90-boat ILCA 6 start. Right after the starting signal the committee boat hoists a yellow-and-blue triangular pennant — First Substitute — and sounds two horns. What does it mean and when will the new warning signal be?
a: General recall — everybody returns; the new warning signal is made one minute after First Substitute is lowered, with one sound
o: Individual recall — only the boats that were over must return; the race continues for the rest
General recall — the new warning signal is made immediately when the pennant is lowered
Postponement — the sequence starts again five minutes after the pennant is lowered
why: Rule 29.2: general recall is First Substitute with two sounds; the warning signal for the new start is made 1 minute after it is removed, with one sound.

q: After a general recall of your 470 fleet, First Substitute is still flying and boats are milling around behind the line. Your crew asks whether you are still "racing" in the sense of the rules while you wait. Are you?
a: No — the general recall ended racing; you will be racing again from the new preparatory signal
o: Yes — you have been racing since the first preparatory signal and remain so until you finish
Yes — you are racing until First Substitute is lowered
No — you will be racing again only when you cross the starting line in the new start
why: Definition Racing: a boat stops racing when a general recall is signalled, and is racing again from her next preparatory signal.

q: In the final seconds before a P-flag start you, to windward, touched Grey's leeward boat and broke rule 11. You start your two turns; halfway through them the committee signals a general recall. Grey hails that you still owe her a penalty in the restart. Do you?
a: No — after a general recall a breach in the original start is not penalised unless it was under rule 2, 30.2, 30.4, 69 or caused injury or serious damage under rule 14
o: Yes — a penalty started before the recall must be completed before the new preparatory signal
Yes — the breach carries over and you must take two turns after the new start
No — but you must retire from the restarted race because you did not complete the penalty
why: Rule 36: a breach in the original start is not penalised in the restart, except under rules 2, 30.2, 30.4, 69 or rule 14 with injury or serious damage.

q: At a national championship the line is 400 m long and 15 boats are over at the gun; the race officer can see that many are over but cannot read their numbers. The pin boat radios two numbers only. What may the race committee do?
a: Signal a general recall — rule 29.2 allows it when the committee is unable to identify the boats that were on the course side
o: Nothing — a general recall is allowed only when there has been an error in the starting procedure
Score every boat in the front row OCS, since it cannot tell them apart
Signal an individual recall and let the protest committee identify the boats afterwards
why: Rule 29.2: when the RC cannot identify the boats that were OCS or subject to rule 30, or erred in the starting procedure, it may signal a general recall.

q: Two classes: 420s at 13:00 and 29ers scheduled at 13:05. The 420 start is general-recalled at 13:00:05. The 29er sailors want their start at 13:05 as published. What does rule 29.2 say about the order of the starts?
a: The 420s get a new start one minute after First Substitute is lowered, and the 29er start follows that new start
o: The 29ers start at 13:05 as scheduled and the 420s are restarted after them
Both classes are restarted together with a single warning signal
The 29er start is cancelled for the day because the 420s were recalled
why: Rule 29.2: the new warning for the recalled class is 1 minute after First Substitute is removed, and the starts of succeeding classes follow the new start.

q: After a general recall of your fleet, First Substitute is lowered with one sound at exactly 12:08:00. With the standard sequence and no further signals, when is your new starting signal?
a: 12:14:00 — warning at 12:09, preparatory at 12:10, one-minute at 12:13
o: 12:13:00 — the new sequence starts at once when the pennant comes down
12:09:00 — the lowering of First Substitute is itself the warning signal
12:15:00 — the fleet gets a full two minutes before the new warning
why: Rule 29.2: the warning signal is made 1 minute after First Substitute is removed; rule 26: start 5 minutes after the warning.

q: I-flag start, a 29er regatta in 15 knots. Forty seconds before the start you are pushed over the line near the middle; you dip straight back behind it and start with the fleet at the gun. The committee shows flag X and later scores you OCS. Is the committee right?
a: Yes — under flag I a boat on the course side in the last minute must sail across an extension of the line, round an end, to the pre-start side before she starts; dipping back does not count
o: No — you were behind the line at the gun and started correctly, so flag X did not apply to you
No — flag X is for boats over at the signal only; a boat over earlier gets a 20 % penalty instead
Yes, but only because you did not return within the four minutes that flag X was displayed
why: Rule 30.1: in the last minute a boat over the line must return across an extension to the pre-start side before starting; rule 29.1 recalls her; otherwise OCS.

fig.note: Flag I: over at 0:40, dipped back, started

q: Flag I is the preparatory signal for your J/70 fleet. With 1 minute 30 seconds to go you find yourself a length over the line while checking the pin-end transit. You bear away and are back behind the line by 1 minute 10 seconds, then start normally. Any penalty?
a: No — rule 30.1 applies only during the last minute before the start; before that you may return across the line itself
o: Yes — under flag I any boat that crosses the line after the preparatory signal must round an end
Yes — you are scored OCS unless you sailed round the pin or the committee boat
No, but you must take a one-turn penalty for crossing the line early
why: Rule 30.1 concerns a boat on the course side "during the last minute before her starting signal"; earlier she may return any way she likes.

fig.note: 1:30 to go, you are over near the pin and bearing away

q: I-flag start at a Bodrum regatta. With 30 seconds to go your bow is over near the pin. You bear away, sail round the outside of the pin to the pre-start side, come back up and cross the line 25 seconds after the gun. Flag X was displayed. Did you start correctly?
a: Yes — you crossed an extension of the line to the pre-start side, as rule 30.1 requires, and then started
o: No — under flag I you had to go round the committee-boat end, not the pin
No — flag X means you were scored OCS the moment it was displayed
Yes, but you are still penalised 20 % for being over in the last minute
why: Rule 30.1: a boat over in the last minute sails across an extension to the pre-start side before she starts — either end will do; then definition Start applies.

fig.note: Round the pin to the pre-start side, then start

q: I-flag start. Fifty seconds before the gun Yellow is clearly over the line; she dips back and is behind the line at the starting signal. Flag X goes up with one sound anyway. Yellow's skipper argues that flag X is only for boats over at the signal. Why did the committee display it?
a: Because rule 29.1 also covers a boat that must comply with rule 30.1 — Yellow still has to sail round an end before she can start
o: The committee made an error — flag X may only be displayed for boats over at the starting signal
Because under flag I every boat that was over at any time after the preparatory signal is OCS
Because flag X under flag I means a 20 % scoring penalty for Yellow
why: Rule 29.1: flag X is displayed when a boat is over at the signal OR must comply with rule 30.1, and stays up until she has complied.

q: Z-flag start, 50 ILCA 7s. With 40 seconds to go your bow pokes over the line in the middle; you bear away, are back behind it at 20 seconds and start with the fleet. You finish 8th. What happens to your score?
a: You receive a 20 % scoring penalty without a hearing — being in the triangle in the last minute is enough, even though you were behind at the gun
o: Nothing — you were behind the line at the starting signal, so you started correctly
You are scored OCS because you did not return round an end of the line
You are disqualified without a hearing unless the race is restarted
why: Rule 30.2: under flag Z a boat identified in the triangle in the last minute gets a 20 % scoring penalty under 44.3(c) without a hearing.

fig.note: Flag Z: over at 0:40, back by 0:20

q: Flag Z is flying for a Dragon start. At 1 minute 30 seconds to go you are a boat length over the line checking the transit; by 1 minute 05 seconds your whole hull is back behind it, and you start cleanly. Has the Z-flag penalty been triggered?
a: No — rule 30.2 applies only to the last minute before the starting signal; you were back in time
o: Yes — under flag Z a boat may not cross the line at any time after the preparatory signal
Yes — the 20 % penalty applies from the preparatory signal onward
No, but you must sail round an end of the line before you may start
why: Rule 30.2: no part of the hull may be in the triangle "during the last minute before her starting signal" — earlier excursions do not count.

q: Z-flag start, 30 boats entered. You are identified in the triangle in the last minute, start correctly and finish 5th. The sailing instructions do not change rule 44.3(c). What is your race score?
a: 11.2 points — 5 plus 20 % of 31 (the DNF score), which is 6.2
o: 6 points — 5 plus 20 % of your own finishing place, rounded up
31 points — a Z-flag boat is scored as if she had not finished
11 points — 6.2 is rounded to a whole number and added to your 5th
why: Rule 44.3(c): the penalty is 20 % of the score for DNF (entries + 1), rounded to the nearest tenth of a point (0.05 upward), added to the boat's score; not worse than DNF.

q: Z-flag start of a 420 fleet. You are identified over the line with 30 seconds to go; at the gun the committee signals a general recall. In the restart you start cleanly. Your crew says the recall wiped the penalty. Did it?
a: No — the Z-flag penalty stands even if the race is restarted; if you are identified again in the restart you get an additional 20 %
o: Yes — a general recall cancels all starting penalties from that attempt
Yes — only the black-flag penalty survives a general recall
No — and you may not sail in the restart at all
why: Rule 30.2: the penalty applies even if the race is restarted or resailed; a boat identified again in a later start gets another 20 %.

q: Z-flag start on a lake in a dying breeze. You were over the line with 45 seconds to go and the committee noted your number. Twenty seconds before the starting signal the race committee postpones with AP and two sounds. Does the 20 % penalty apply in the race when it is finally sailed?
a: No — the Z-flag penalty does not apply if the race is postponed or abandoned before the starting signal
o: Yes — the penalty applies to the race whenever it is eventually started
Yes — a postponement counts as a restart, and the penalty survives restarts
No — because the race committee must display your sail number first
why: Rule 30.2: the penalty applies if the race is restarted or resailed, but not if it is postponed or abandoned before the starting signal.

q: Z-flag start, Saronic Gulf. In the last 30 seconds you are to the left of the pin, outside the line, and your bow is over the line's extension beyond the pin. At the gun you are still there. Do you get the 20 % penalty, and have you started?
a: No Z-flag penalty — you were not inside the triangle between the ends of the line and the first mark; but you have not started and must return to the pre-start side and cross the line
o: 20 % penalty — any part of the hull over the line or its extensions in the last minute triggers rule 30.2
No penalty and no problem — you were beyond the pin, so you may simply bear away onto the beat
20 % penalty and OCS — both apply to a boat over the extension
why: Rule 30.2 covers only the triangle formed by the ends of the line and the first mark; a boat beyond the pin is outside it, but she still has to start.

fig.note: Over the extension beyond the pin, outside the triangle

q: U-flag start of a J/70 fleet in 18 knots. You are identified inside the triangle with 20 seconds to go. The race is not recalled and you sail it, finishing 2nd. What will the results show?
a: UFD — disqualified without a hearing under rule 30.3
o: ZFP — a 20 % scoring penalty added to your 2nd place
OCS — unless you returned and started correctly
2nd — the U flag only applies if there is a general recall
why: Rule 30.3: under flag U a boat identified in the triangle in the last minute is disqualified without a hearing unless the race is restarted or resailed.

fig.note: Flag U: in the triangle 20 s before the gun

q: U-flag start, 80 Optimists. You are identified in the triangle in the last minute, but at the gun the race committee signals a general recall. May you start in the restart, and with what penalty?
a: Yes, with no penalty — the U-flag disqualification does not apply when the race is restarted
o: No — your sail number will be displayed and you must not sail in the restart
Yes, but you carry a 20 % scoring penalty into the restart
Yes, but only after taking a two-turns penalty before the new preparatory signal
why: Rule 30.3: the boat is disqualified without a hearing "unless the race is restarted or resailed" — unlike the black flag.

q: U-flag start. You were identified in the triangle 15 seconds before the gun, kept sailing and are leading on the first beat when the committee abandons the race with flag N because the windward mark has dragged. The race is resailed an hour later. Does your U-flag disqualification carry into the resail?
a: No — rule 30.3 does not apply when the race is restarted or resailed; you may sail the resail without penalty
o: Yes — the disqualification was earned in the original start and stands
Yes — unless you were not identified in the resail as well
No — but you must get the race committee's permission before starting
why: Rule 30.3: disqualification without a hearing unless the race is restarted or resailed; rule 36 confirms the breach is not carried over.

q: Black-flag start. You are identified in the triangle with 40 seconds to go; the race is sailed through. No flag X was displayed after the starting signal and you argue at the race office that you were never recalled, so the BFD cannot stand. Is the argument good?
a: No — when rule 30.4 applies to a boat, rule 29.1 does not; the committee did not have to recall you, only to identify you
o: Yes — without flag X and one sound a boat cannot be scored for a starting error
Yes — the black flag only applies after a general recall, so the first start must use flag X
No — but the committee should have displayed your number before the start
why: Rule 29.1 (last sentence): if rule 29.2, 30.3 or 30.4 applies, rule 29.1 does not — no individual recall is signalled for a boat penalised under the black flag.

q: Black-flag start of a 100-boat ILCA 6 fleet. You are identified in the triangle with 15 seconds to go; at the gun a general recall is signalled. What happens to you?
a: You are disqualified without a hearing; the committee displays your sail number before the next warning signal and you must not sail in the restart
o: Nothing — a general recall cancels the black-flag penalty like any other starting penalty
You get a 20 % scoring penalty and may sail the restart
You may sail the restart; the disqualification applies only if the race is not recalled
why: Rule 30.4: disqualification without a hearing, surviving a general recall; after a recall the RC displays her sail number and she shall not sail in the restart.

q: After a black-flag general recall your sail number 183455 is displayed on the committee boat. You sail the restart anyway and finish 3rd. The results show DSQ. May you discard this result as your worst race of the series?
a: No — a boat that sails the restart after her number was displayed gets a disqualification that is not excludable from her series score
o: Yes — a black-flag disqualification is excludable like any other DSQ
Yes — because you finished the race, the normal discard rules apply
No — because a black-flag disqualification is never excludable, whether or not you sail the restart
why: Rule 30.4: if a boat whose number was displayed sails in the restart or resail, her disqualification shall not be excluded.

fig.title: After the recall
lines: Your number displayed on the RC boat

q: Black-flag start of a 49er fleet. You are identified over the line with 35 seconds to go. Then, 10 seconds before the starting signal, the wind dies completely and the race committee postpones with AP. When the race is eventually started an hour later, are you still black-flagged?
a: No — the black-flag penalty does not apply if the race is postponed or abandoned before the starting signal
o: Yes — the black flag was flying when you were identified, and that is what counts
Yes — the penalty survives restarts, resails and postponements alike
No — but only if the race committee forgets to display your number
why: Rule 30.4: the penalty applies if the race is restarted or resailed, but not if it is postponed or abandoned before the starting signal.

q: Black-flag start at a Mediterranean championship. Thirty seconds before the gun your bow is over near the committee boat; you duck back, start behind the fleet and sail a fine race to 6th. No general recall was signalled. What is your result?
a: BFD — disqualified without a hearing; returning behind the line does not undo a black-flag breach
o: 6th — you were behind the line at the starting signal and started correctly
OCS — because you did not round an end of the line before starting
6th with a 20 % scoring penalty added
why: Rule 30.4: no part of the hull may be in the triangle in the last minute; a boat identified doing so is disqualified without a hearing.

fig.note: Black flag, 30 s to go, bow over near the RC boat

q: Black-flag general recall. Your number appears on the board on the committee boat, but you are certain you were behind the line in the last minute — your GPS track and a coach boat confirm it. The restart is in a few minutes. What should you do?
a: Do not sail the restart; afterwards request redress with your evidence — sailing it would make the disqualification non-excludable
o: Sail the restart — if you were not over, the disqualification cannot stand anyway
Sail the restart and protest the race committee on the water with a red flag
Accept the disqualification — a black-flag decision cannot be reviewed
why: Rule 30.4: a boat whose number is displayed shall not sail the restart; if she does, her DSQ is not excludable. An RC error is a redress ground (61.4(b)(1)).

fig.title: Black-flag recall
lines: Your number on the RC board
GPS track shows you behind the line

q: Black-flag start. You are identified in the triangle 50 seconds before the gun. The race starts, but 20 minutes later it is abandoned because the wind dies. The committee announces the race will be resailed tomorrow. What is your position for the resail?
a: The committee must display your sail number before the next warning signal for that race, and you may not sail the resail — the penalty applies to a resailed race
o: You may sail the resail — abandonment after the start wipes all penalties from the original race
You may sail the resail with a 20 % scoring penalty
You may sail the resail because the committee did not display your number during the original race
why: Rule 30.4: if the race is abandoned after the starting signal, the RC displays her sail number before the next warning signal and she shall not sail the resail.

q: Black-flag start with 120 boats. You know you were over the line with 20 seconds to go, but the line was so crowded that the race committee could not identify anyone and signalled a general recall. No sail numbers are displayed. May you sail the restart?
a: Yes — rule 30.4 penalises a boat that is identified; with no number displayed you may sail the restart, though you must stay out of the triangle in its last minute
o: No — a boat that knows she was over must retire from the restart even if not identified
No — after a black-flag general recall the whole front row is automatically disqualified
Yes, but you must take a two-turns penalty before the new preparatory signal
why: Rule 30.4: "if a boat is identified" she is disqualified and her number displayed; a boat not identified has no penalty under 30.4 for that start.

q: You coach a youth team and want them to remember which starting penalties survive a general recall. In the last minute a boat is identified over the line, then the committee signals a general recall. Under which preparatory flags may she sail the restart?
a: Under P, I, U and Z she may sail the restart (with a 20 % penalty under Z); only under the black flag may she not
o: Under P and I only — Z, U and black all exclude her from the restart
Under all of them — a general recall wipes every starting penalty
Under P and Z only — I, U and black all exclude her from the restart
why: Rule 30: only the black flag (30.4) excludes an identified boat from the restart; Z (30.2) adds 20 % but lets her sail; U (30.3) is cancelled by a restart.

q: Reading the results after a championship day you see "BFD" against your sail number in race 4. What does it mean?
a: Disqualified under rule 30.4 — identified in the triangle in the last minute of a black-flag start
o: Did not finish within the time limit
A 20 % scoring penalty for being over in the last minute under flag Z
Broke rule 30.1 — failed to return round an end under flag I
why: Appendix A scoring abbreviations: BFD is a disqualification under rule 30.4 (black flag).

q: The provisional results of a 24-boat J/24 regatta show you "OCS" in race 2. What does that mean, and how many points is it?
a: You did not start — part of your hull was on the course side at the starting signal and you did not return; 25 points (entries plus one)
o: You started correctly but finished outside the time limit; 24 points
You were disqualified after a hearing for a Part 2 breach; 25 points
You started late, more than 4 minutes after the signal; 0 points
why: Appendix A: OCS means on the course side at the starting signal and failed to start, or broke rule 30.1; scored as entries + 1.

q: Twenty seconds before the start you are reaching along the line on starboard towards the committee boat, planning to squeeze in at the stern. Blue, to leeward and overlapped, also on starboard, luffs to close-hauled and there is no longer a gap between her and the committee boat. She hails "No room!" What are your rights?
a: None at the committee boat — at a starting mark surrounded by navigable water rule 18 does not apply; under rule 11 you must keep clear of Blue, even if it means going behind the committee boat
o: You are entitled to mark-room — you are inside and overlapped when you reach the committee boat
Blue must hold her course — a leeward boat may not luff within three hull lengths of a starting mark
You may hold your course and Blue must bear away because you hailed for room first
why: Section C preamble: rule 18 does not apply at a starting mark surrounded by navigable water while boats approach it to start; rule 11: windward keeps clear.
ref: RRS Part 2 Section C preamble, RRS 11

fig.note: 20 s to go; Blue is leeward and luffing

q: Pin-end start in a 470 fleet. Ten seconds before the gun you approach the pin on port tack, intending to tack onto starboard right at the mark. Grey is coming at the pin close-hauled on starboard. You hail "Room at the mark!" Who must keep clear?
a: You — rule 10 applies, and there is no mark-room at a starting mark surrounded by navigable water; port keeps clear of starboard
o: Grey — you are the inside boat at the pin and so entitled to mark-room under rule 18
Grey — you hailed first, so she must give you room to tack at the mark
Nobody — before the starting signal the rules of Part 2 are not yet in force
why: Section C preamble: no mark-room at a starting mark surrounded by navigable water; rule 10: port keeps clear of starboard; Part 2 applies from the prep signal.
ref: RRS 10, RRS Part 2 Section C preamble

fig.note: 10 s to go at the pin

q: Forty seconds before the start, Red comes from clear astern and becomes overlapped to leeward of you, a hull length away. She then luffs steadily above close-hauled, pushing you up towards the line. You protest that she is sailing above her proper course. Is Red breaking rule 17?
a: No — before the starting signal a boat has no proper course, so rule 17 cannot limit her; she may luff, but under rule 16.1 she must give you room to keep clear
o: Yes — a leeward boat that gained her overlap from clear astern may not sail above close-hauled
Yes — rule 17 applies from the preparatory signal onward
No — because she is more than a hull length away rule 17 does not apply, and she may luff as hard as she likes
why: Definition Proper Course: a boat has none before her starting signal, so rule 17 does not restrict her; rules 11 and 16.1 govern the luff.
ref: RRS definition Proper Course, RRS 17, RRS 16.1

fig.note: 40 s to go; Red is luffing from leeward

q: You are the leeward boat, close-hauled on starboard, setting up to start by the committee boat. Black, overlapped to windward, is barging in and hails "Mark-room — give me room at the committee boat!" If you hold your close-hauled course she will not fit. What should you do?
a: Hold your course — Black gets no mark-room at a starting mark and must keep clear of you under rule 11; if you change course, give her room to keep clear
o: Bear away to let her in — an inside overlapped boat is entitled to mark-room at any mark, the committee boat included
Luff hard to head to wind to push her into the committee boat — she is windward and must keep clear whatever you do
Tack away — a boat that hails for room at a mark must be given it, whoever has right of way
why: Section C preamble: no mark-room at a starting mark surrounded by navigable water; rule 11: windward keeps clear; your course changes are subject to rule 16.1.
ref: RRS Part 2 Section C preamble, RRS 11, RRS 16.1

fig.note: Black is barging at the RC boat

q: Five seconds before the gun you are to windward of Green, both on starboard, half a length from the committee boat's stern. Green suddenly luffs to head to wind; the only way to keep clear of her is to hit the committee boat, which you do. Who broke which rule?
a: Green broke rule 16.1 — she changed course without giving you room to keep clear; you touched a starting mark, but you were compelled to and may be exonerated
o: Only you — a windward boat must keep clear whatever the leeward boat does, and you touched the mark
Only Green — a leeward boat may never luff above close-hauled near the committee boat
Nobody — contact with the committee boat before the start carries no penalty
why: Rule 16.1: a right-of-way boat changing course gives room to keep clear, including space to comply with rule 31; rule 43.1(a) exonerates the compelled boat.

fig.note: 5 s to go; Green luffs to head to wind

q: Fifteen seconds before the start of a Star-class race, squeezing in at the committee-boat end, your quarter brushes the committee boat's topsides. No other boat was involved and there is no damage. What must you do?
a: Take a one-turn penalty as soon as possible after getting well clear — you touched a starting mark while racing
o: Nothing — a boat is not racing before the starting signal, so rule 31 does not apply
Take a two-turns penalty — touching the committee boat is a Part 2 breach
Retire — touching the committee boat before the start is a disqualification
why: Rule 31: while racing (from the preparatory signal) a boat shall not touch a starting mark before starting; rule 44.1: a One-Turn Penalty for rule 31.

fig.note: 15 s to go; your quarter touches the RC boat

q: P-flag start, light wind, a strong favourable current pushing the fleet over. You plan a "dip start": sit on the course side of the line before the gun, then after the starting signal dip back across the line to the pre-start side and cross again. Is this legal?
a: Yes — under flag P you may return across the line itself; you start when your hull crosses after being entirely on the pre-start side after the signal
o: No — a boat on the course side at the starting signal must always sail round an end of the line
No — a boat on the course side in the last minute is disqualified without a hearing
Yes, but you must first take a two-turns penalty for being over the line
why: Definition Start: a boat starts when her hull crosses the line after being entirely on the pre-start side after the signal; only flag I requires an end.

fig.note: Flag P; dip back after the gun, then start

q: Same tactic, different day: the preparatory flag is I. You sit above the line, and after the gun you dip back across the middle of the line and start again. The committee boat scores you OCS. Why?
a: Because under flag I a boat on the course side in the last minute must return across an extension of the line — round an end — before she starts; dipping the line does not comply
o: Because under flag I a boat may not be on the course side at any time after the preparatory signal
Because the dip start is forbidden under every preparatory flag
Because under flag I you get a 20 % penalty, which the committee records as OCS
why: Rule 30.1, definition Start: a boat subject to rule 30.1 has not started until she has crossed an extension to the pre-start side and then crossed the line.

q: Four and a half minutes before the start of a Hobie 16 race — thirty seconds after the warning signal — you misjudge a gybe and your hull bumps the pin-end buoy. Your crew wants to do a penalty turn. Do you owe one?
a: No — you are not yet racing; racing begins at the preparatory signal, and rule 31 applies only while racing
o: Yes — a one-turn penalty, because you touched a starting mark
Yes — a two-turns penalty, because touching a mark before the start is more serious
No — touching the pin never carries a penalty, only touching the committee boat does
why: Definition Racing: a boat is racing from her preparatory signal; rule 31 applies to a boat racing — before the preparatory signal there is no penalty.

fig.note: 4:30 to go, before the preparatory signal

q: Thirty seconds before the start you are sitting on the line, head to wind, and back your jib to drift astern and open a gap to leeward. White, close-hauled on starboard behind you, has to bear away sharply to avoid your transom. Who had to keep clear?
a: You — a boat moving astern through the water by backing a sail keeps clear of a boat that is not
o: White — she was clear astern and must keep clear of a boat ahead
White — a boat head to wind holds her position and others must avoid her
Nobody — before the starting signal boats may manoeuvre as they wish
why: Rule 21.3: a boat moving astern, or sideways to windward, through the water by backing a sail shall keep clear of one that is not.

fig.note: You are backing the jib and drifting astern

q: The sailing instructions of a club series say: "A boat that does not start within 4 minutes after her starting signal will be scored DNS without a hearing." A tangled spinnaker sheet keeps you behind the line, and you finally cross it 5 minutes after the gun. You sail the course and finish 9th. What is your score?
a: DNS — the sailing instructions set a time limit for starting, and you crossed after it
o: 9th — a late start is not a breach of any rule
DNF — you started, but outside the time limit, so you count as not finishing
9th with a 20 % penalty for starting late
why: Rules 25 and 90.2: the SI may set a starting time limit; a boat that does not start within it is scored as the SI say — here DNS (rule A5).

q: The sailing instructions say: "No warning signal will be made after 15:30." The committee boat makes the warning signal for race 4 at 15:40. You had already started home and miss the race. What is your remedy, if any?
a: Request redress — making a warning signal after the time stated in the sailing instructions is an improper action of the race committee
o: None — the race committee may start a race at any time it considers fair
Protest the race committee with a red flag at the next opportunity
None — you should have stayed on the water until the committee boat went in
why: Rule 61.4(b)(1): redress for a score made significantly worse by an improper action of the RC — here a warning signal made contrary to the SI.

fig.title: SI: no warning after 15:30
lines: You had left for the harbour

q: Two classes start five minutes apart. The first class has just started and flag X is flying for its OCS boats. Your class flag is up and your preparatory flag goes up a minute later. A nervous crew asks whether flag X means your sequence is interrupted. Does it?
a: No — flag X is the individual recall for the class that has just started; your sequence continues as signalled
o: Yes — while flag X is flying no other class may be in sequence
Yes — flag X cancels the warning signal and your class will be restarted
No, but your start is delayed until flag X is lowered
why: Rule 29.1: flag X recalls the boats over at the previous start; rule 26: the next class's sequence is made with or after that start and continues.

fig.title: Two classes
lines: First class started, flag X up
Your class flag up, then P up

q: A 60-boat ILCA 7 start. Flag X goes up with one sound. You were in the front row, sighting the pin against the committee boat's flagstaff, and are confident your bow was behind the line. Four boats near you go back. Should you?
a: If you are sure your hull was behind the line, keep racing — flag X concerns only the boats that were over; if you are scored OCS anyway, request redress
o: Yes — when flag X is displayed every boat in the front row must return to be safe, whether or not she was over
Yes — flag X means the committee could not identify the boats, so the whole fleet is recalled
No, and you cannot be scored OCS later because your sail number was not hailed by the committee
why: Rule 29.1: the recall is for boats whose hull was over at the signal; the RC may still score a boat OCS (A5); an RC error is corrected by redress (61.4(b)(1)).

q: You were a metre over at the gun of a 420 race. The committee boat was slow: flag X went up 40 seconds after the starting signal, by which time you were two hundred metres up the beat. You return and start, losing most of the fleet. Were you obliged to return, and do you have a claim?
a: Yes — your duty to start correctly does not depend on the flag; the late signal is an improper action of the committee and may ground redress
o: No — flag X must be displayed promptly; shown late, it has no effect and you had started correctly
No — once you are more than three hull lengths past the line an individual recall no longer applies to you
Yes, and there is no possible claim — the timing of flag X is entirely at the committee's discretion
why: Rule 29.1: the RC shall display flag X promptly; definition Start: she has not started until she returns; 61.4(b)(1): an improper RC action may ground redress.

q: P-flag start, you are OCS at the pin end. Instead of dipping back across the line through the crowd, you bear away round the outside of the pin and sail across the line's extension until your whole hull is on the pre-start side, then tack and cross the line. Have you returned correctly?
a: Yes — under flag P the hull need only be entirely on the pre-start side of the line or its extensions before you start; either route is fine
o: No — under flag P a recalled boat must return across the line itself, not an extension
No — only a boat under flag I may go round the pin to return
Yes, but you must also take a one-turn penalty for passing the pin on the wrong side
why: Rule 29.1: the hull must be completely on the pre-start side of the line or one of its extensions; definition Start applies when she then crosses the line.

fig.note: Round the pin, across the extension, then start

q: At the preparatory signal of an Optimist start the committee boat hoists flag Z and, below it, flag I. Your coach had told you about them separately. Which rules apply in the last minute?
a: Both rule 30.1 and rule 30.2 — a boat over in the last minute must return round an end and also gets a 20 % scoring penalty
o: Only rule 30.2 — flag I is cancelled when it is displayed with flag Z
Only rule 30.1 — flag Z is a reminder that the penalty is 20 % if you fail to return
Rule 30.3 — the two flags together mean the same as flag U
why: Rule 26: the preparatory signal may be "Z with I"; race signals: flag I means rule 30.1 applies and flag Z means rule 30.2 applies — both at once.

q: At a regatta with Optimists starting first and 29ers second, the 29er class flag goes up with one sound 30 seconds before the Optimist starting signal. The 29er fleet is confused. Is this signal in accordance with the rules?
a: No — the warning signal for a succeeding class shall be made with or after the starting signal of the preceding class
o: Yes — the race committee may overlap sequences as long as the preparatory signals do not coincide
Yes — a warning signal may be made at any time once the previous class is in its last minute
No — the warning signal of the next class must be made exactly five minutes after the previous start
why: Rule 26: the warning signal for each succeeding class shall be made with or after the starting signal of the preceding class.

q: Lasers start at 12:05 and 470s follow. You are in a 470 and see flag P go up for your class at 12:06:00 with one sound. With the standard sequence, when is your start, and when will P come down?
a: Start at 12:10:00; flag P comes down at 12:09:00 with one long sound
o: Start at 12:11:00; flag P comes down at 12:10:00
Start at 12:09:00; flag P comes down at 12:08:00
Start at 12:10:00; flag P comes down at the starting signal
why: Rule 26: the preparatory signal is 4 minutes before the start and the preparatory flag is lowered 1 minute before the start.

q: The first race is scheduled for 11:00. At 10:55 the committee boat displays AP over numeral pennant 1 with two sounds. At what time should you now expect the warning signal, with a standard sequence?
a: 11:55 — the start is postponed one hour to 12:00 and the warning signal is 5 minutes before it
o: 10:56 — the warning signal is made one minute after AP is displayed
12:05 — the warning signal is one hour after the original one
11:00 — AP over a numeral pennant only postpones the start, not the warning
why: Race signals: AP over numeral pennant 1 postpones the race 1 hour from the scheduled start; rule 26: the warning is 5 min before the start.
ref: RRS 26, race signals (AP over numeral pennant)

lines: AP over numeral pennant 1, two sounds

q: A river start with 2 knots of current running towards the course. In the last 10 seconds the wind dies, you lose steerage and the current carries your bow over the line at the gun. Flag X goes up. You feel it was not your fault. What is your position?
a: You are OCS whatever the cause — return to the pre-start side and start; current or lack of wind is no ground for redress
o: You started correctly — a boat without steerage way cannot be OCS
You may keep racing and ask for redress because the current, not you, moved the boat
You must retire — a boat carried over by current cannot return
why: Definition Start and rule 29.1 look only at where the hull was at the starting signal; rule 61.4 gives no redress for weather or current.

fig.note: Current sets towards the course; no steerage

q: The sailing instructions say: "The preparatory signal will be flag P unless flag U or the black flag is displayed." At four minutes you see flag P. If you find yourself over the line in the last 30 seconds, what must you do?
a: Get your whole hull back behind the line by any route and start after the starting signal — under flag P there is no extra penalty
o: Sail round an end of the line before starting — otherwise you are OCS
Accept a 20 % scoring penalty, which applies to any boat over in the last minute
Retire — you will be disqualified without a hearing
why: Under flag P only the definition Start applies: be entirely on the pre-start side at or after the signal, then cross; rules 30.1–30.4 need I, Z, U or black.

q: After a general recall of your Finn fleet, First Substitute is flying and you drift about waiting. Before the new preparatory signal you misjudge a tack and your transom touches the pin. A rival hails "Penalty!" Do you owe one?
a: No — the general recall ended racing, and you are not racing again until the new preparatory signal; rule 31 does not apply
o: Yes — a one-turn penalty, because the pin is a starting mark
Yes — because you have been racing continuously since the first preparatory signal
No — but only because the pin was touched by the transom and not the bow
why: Definition Racing: racing ends at a general recall and resumes at the next preparatory signal; rule 31 applies only to a boat racing.

fig.note: First Substitute flying; before the new preparatory signal

q: AP has been flying for twenty minutes. The committee lowers it with one sound, and you start your watch for the warning signal — but ten seconds later AP goes up again with two sounds. What now?
a: The race is postponed again — no warning signal will be made until one minute after AP is next lowered
o: The warning signal is still due one minute after the first lowering — the second AP is for the next class
The sequence has started — the second AP counts as the warning signal
Racing is over for the day — AP displayed twice means AP over A
why: Race signals, AP: the warning will be made 1 minute after removal "unless at that time the race is postponed again or abandoned".

q: Just after the starting signal of your race the committee boat hoists a white flag with a blue St Andrew's cross and makes one sound. What does it mean?
a: Individual recall — one or more boats were over the line and must return to start
o: General recall — the whole fleet returns for a new start
Shortened course — finish at the next mark
Abandonment — return to the starting area
why: Rule 29.1 and race signals: flag X with one sound is the individual recall.

q: Seconds after the gun, the committee boat hoists a triangular pennant with blue and yellow vertical panels and sounds two horns. The leaders are already pointing at the first mark. What has happened?
a: General recall — the whole fleet returns and the class will be restarted
o: Individual recall — only the boats that were over must return
The race is abandoned for the day
The course has been changed — watch for a new compass bearing
why: Rule 29.2 and race signals: First Substitute with two sounds is the general recall.

q: You started your watch at the warning signal. It reads 4:00 when you see flag P come down and hear a long sound. At what reading will the starting signal be made?
a: 5:00 — the preparatory flag comes down one minute before the start
o: 4:30 — the long sound is the thirty-second signal
6:00 — the start is two minutes after the preparatory flag comes down
8:00 — the preparatory flag comes down four minutes before the start
why: Rule 26: the warning is at 5 minutes and the preparatory flag is removed at 1 minute, so the start is 60 s after it comes down.

q: A Dragon start. The class flag went up at 14:00:00 and flag P at 14:01:00. You look up and see flag P being lowered. What time is it, and when is the starting signal?
a: 14:04:00 now; the starting signal is at 14:05:00
o: 14:05:00 now; this is the starting signal
14:03:00 now; the starting signal is at 14:05:00
14:04:00 now; the starting signal is at 14:06:00
why: Rule 26: warning 5 min, preparatory 4 min, preparatory flag down 1 min before the start.

q: During a Melges 24 sequence the committee boat lowers flag P by mistake at three minutes to go, with a long sound, then hoists it again twenty seconds later. Half the fleet now has the wrong time. What may the race committee properly do, and what should you expect?
a: There has been an error in the starting procedure — the committee may postpone before the start or signal a general recall after it; expect AP or First Substitute
o: Nothing — once the preparatory signal has been made the sequence must run to the starting signal
Hail the correct time to the fleet — a hail replaces the visual signals
Score every boat that starts on the wrong time OCS without a hearing
why: Rule 27.3 allows postponement before the start for any reason; rule 29.2 allows a general recall when there has been an error in the starting procedure.

fig.title: Sequence error
lines: 3:00 to go: flag P lowered by mistake
3:00 to go minus 20 s: flag P re-hoisted

q: You were OCS and are sailing back to the line on port tack after the gun. Blue, close-hauled on starboard, has started correctly. You misjudge her speed and your bow hits her quarter — a scuff, no damage. Who broke which rules?
a: You broke rule 21.1 (and rule 10) and rule 14; Blue, the right-of-way boat, is exonerated for the contact because there was no damage or injury
o: Blue broke rule 14 — a right-of-way boat must always avoid contact, and she did not
Nobody — contact without damage between a returning boat and a starter is ignored
Both equally — each boat broke rule 14 and each must take a two-turns penalty
why: Rule 21.1: a returning boat keeps clear; rule 14: she must avoid contact; rule 43.1(c): the right-of-way boat is exonerated under 14 absent damage or injury.
